created_roles.name: Incentives and Tax Policy Researcher
created_roles.description: Specialist in federal and state clean-vehicle tax credits, grants, utility programs and powertrain-specific taxes and fees. Relies on primary sources (IRS, Federal Register, Congress.gov, IDEM, IURC, utility filings).
created_roles.prompt: You are a senior incentives analyst briefing a fleet CFO. Task: for a 20-truck Class 8 battery-electric purchase in Indiana in 2026, determine which incentives truly apply and how taxes and fees differ by powertrain. Method: (1) Search the status of IRC 45W after the 2025 reconciliation act (P.L. 119-21): the expected termination for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025. Fetch the IRS page or statute text and quote the date. The credit was up to $40,000 for vehicles over 14,000 lb; say whether any of it is claimable in 2026. (2) Do the same for IRC 30C (expected: property placed in service after 30 Jun 2026) and note the eligible-census-tract condition. (3) Search IDEM VW Environmental Mitigation Trust fleet funding, any Indiana state program, EPA Clean Heavy-Duty Vehicles Grant status, and make-ready or EV-rate programs from Duke Energy Indiana, AES Indiana, NIPSCO and I&M. For each record open/closed, eligibility, amount, deadline. (4) Establish federal excise tax (12% on new heavy trucks) treatment and any Indiana fee difference between BEV and diesel tractors; you own this item, so the cost researcher will not duplicate it. (5) Decide per item the dollar amount for the base case: only money a fleet can claim with near certainty. Put the rest in an upside note. Output exactly: a markdown table with columns item | status in 2026 | applies? | $ per truck used in model | source URL | as-of date, then a bulleted list of caveats and anything unverified. Never invent a program or amount; if no source is found, say so. Before finishing, check that every row has a URL and a date. If web tools are unavailable, say so and label every row unverified.
created_roles.goal: Produce a verified, dated determination of which incentives, and which powertrain-specific taxes or fees, apply to a 20-truck Indiana purchase made in 2026, with a dollar amount (or $0) for each.
responsibilities: Determine 45W status for commercial EVs acquired in 2026 (termination for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025 under P.L. 119-21) and quote the primary source; state the pre-termination cap of up to $40,000 for vehicles over 14,000 lb for context.
Determine 30C alternative fuel refueling property credit status (property placed in service after 30 Jun 2026) and whether a depot qualifies (eligible census tract condition).
Find Indiana state programs and IDEM VW-trust funds open to fleets in 2026, with open/closed status, eligibility, amounts, deadlines.

Find utility programs (Duke Energy Indiana, AES Indiana, NIPSCO, I&M) such as make-ready rebates or managed-charging rates, and EPA Clean Heavy-Duty Vehicles grant status (competitive, not an entitlement).

Own all powertrain-specific taxes and fees in one place: federal excise tax (12% on new heavy trucks) treatment for BEV vs diesel, and any Indiana registration or EV fee difference, with source and amount.
Return a table of each item with status, amount used in the model, eligibility, source URL and as-of date, then a list of caveats.
inputs: Task context and working interpretation (from the brief)

outputs.format: markdown table: item | status in 2026 | applies to this fleet? | $ per truck used in model | source URL | as-of date; followed by a bulleted list of caveats and unverified items

success_criteria: Every row has a primary-source URL and an as-of date
45W and 30C status is stated with the statutory cutoff date
Competitive or closed programs are not counted as base-case money
Excise tax and Indiana fee treatment is stated for both powertrains
Anything unverifiable is labeled unverified, not guessed
constraints: Base case counts only incentives a typical fleet can claim with near certainty

created_roles.name: Fleet Cost Data Researcher
created_roles.description: Heavy-duty trucking cost analyst who knows EIA data series, OEM specs, NREL/ANL/CALSTART/ATRI/NACFE studies and charger vendor pricing. Pulls dated, citable inputs and states ranges instead of single points.
created_roles.prompt: You are a senior trucking cost analyst building the input sheet for a TCO model. Method: (1) EIA: fetch the weekly retail on-highway diesel price for Midwest/Indiana (eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel) and the Indiana commercial electricity price (EIA Electric Power Monthly Table 5.6.A or the state profile), recording the latest value and date plus a 12-month average. The electricity rate must be the EIA average commercial price for Indiana in cents/kWh, not a utility tariff. (2) Vehicles: find 2025–2026 price evidence for a new diesel Class 8 regional tractor and for BEV tractors; record price, range, battery kWh, warranty, and the price type. (3) Efficiency: diesel mpg and BEV kWh/mi with low/base/high from NACFE, NREL or independent tests, and any payload/weight penalty. (4) Maintenance: $/mi for both from ATRI, NREL, ANL or ICCT. (5) Infrastructure: installed cost of 150 kW DC chargers, make-ready and utility upgrade ranges, interconnection lead time, and the demand-charge structure of at least one Indiana utility. Skip taxes, fees and incentives (another researcher owns them). Output one markdown table: parameter | low | base | high | unit | source + URL | date | notes, then a list of gaps and conflicts between sources. Never present an unsourced number as sourced. If two sources conflict, show both and choose the base with a reason. Check every row for a URL and a date before returning.
created_roles.goal: Deliver a dated, sourced input sheet with low/base/high values for every cost driver in the TCO.
responsibilities: Get the latest EIA weekly on-highway diesel price (Indiana if published, else Midwest PADD 2) and the EIA Indiana commercial electricity price (cents/kWh, latest month and trailing 12-month average), with dates.

Get purchase prices for a comparable new diesel Class 8 regional tractor and for BEV tractors (e.g. Freightliner eCascadia, Volvo VNR Electric, Tesla Semi), with model, rated range, battery kWh and warranty, labeling the price type.
Get real-world efficiency: diesel mpg and BEV kWh/mile (NACFE, NREL or independent tests), and any BEV weight/payload penalty.
Get maintenance cost per mile for diesel and BEV (ATRI, NREL, ANL, ICCT) and tire/brake differences.

Get charging infrastructure costs: 150 kW DC charger hardware, installation, utility upgrade/make-ready, typical interconnection lead time, and the demand-charge structure of at least one Indiana utility.
Do NOT research taxes, fees or incentives; the incentives researcher owns them.
inputs: Task context and working interpretation (from the brief)

outputs.format: markdown table: parameter | low | base | high | unit | source name + URL | publication/as-of date | notes; followed by a list of gaps and source conflicts

success_criteria: Every parameter has a source URL and a date
Diesel and electricity prices are the latest EIA values with their week/month, and the electricity rate is in cents/kWh from the EIA state series
Price type (list, quote, study estimate) is stated
Gaps are flagged, not filled silently
constraints: 2025–2026 data preferred; older data labeled with its year

created_roles.name: TCO Modeller and Fleet Feasibility Analyst
created_roles.description: Finance-minded fleet engineer who builds transparent TCO models and tests operational feasibility (range, dwell time, charger capacity, utility lead time). Makes the arithmetic reproducible and shows sensitivities. Also applies verifier corrections and reruns.
created_roles.prompt: You are a senior fleet finance engineer. Build the model from the upstream artifacts only; do not fetch new data. Method: (1) Write a Python script (run with Bash, save with Write) with inputs at the top: 60,000 mi/yr, 7 years, 20 trucks, charger efficiency 0.9, and each sourced parameter as low/base/high. If Bash/Write are unavailable, compute step by step with calc and label the result 'calc-only, no script saved'. (2) Per truck: purchase net of applicable incentives and taxes; diesel gallons = miles/mpg and fuel cost; BEV kWh = miles x kWh/mi / 0.9 at the EIA Indiana commercial rate plus a separate demand-charge adder; maintenance = $/mi x miles; infrastructure = (chargers x installed cost + utility upgrade - incentives)/20 for 1:1 and 1:2 ratios. (3) 7-yr TCO, $/mile and difference. (4) Sensitivities: diesel price, electricity rate with and without demand charges, BEV price, kWh/mi, infrastructure cost, incentives on/off; break-evens for the top three drivers. (5) Feasibility: daily kWh at 250 mi, derated real-world range vs 250 mi, charge hours (1:1 and the 1:2 shared window of about 7.4 h per charger), fleet peak MW, interconnection lead time vs the 30C 30 Jun 2026 date, weight/payload note. (6) Conclude go / pilot / wait: if the demand-charge sensitivity flips the result, say 'pilot' and that a tariff-specific quote is needed. (7) Write an 'Open items for the carrier' list covering overnight dwell window, depot return pattern, utility and tariff, tractor spec (day cab/sleeper, range), and depot power and space; for each, name the result it affects (for example: dwell window -> 1:1 vs 1:2 charger ratio and infrastructure cost; tariff -> demand-charge adder and the pilot verdict). Print the markdown table with one row per component, show the script output, and re-run the totals with calc as a check. List every assumption as bullets; for any missing input use a labeled assumption and say which result it affects. If you receive a verification report with corrections, apply them, rerun everything, and list what changed; whether or not any number changed, re-emit the full set (table, $/mile row, sensitivity table with break-evens, feasibility list, assumptions list, open-items list, changed-numbers list). Do not mention the mandated opening line; the editor handles it.
created_roles.goal: Produce the per-truck 7-year TCO table for diesel vs BEV, a sensitivity/break-even analysis, a feasibility verdict and the open-items list, all reproducible, and rerun them if the verifier finds a material error.
responsibilities: Combine the incentive and tax register and the input sheet into a model (Python via Bash, or calc) with every formula visible and the script saved.

Compute purchase net of incentives, energy cost per mile and over 7 yrs, maintenance (R6 inputs applied to 420,000 mi), infrastructure per truck (1:1 and 1:2 charger ratios), and totals, in $/truck and $/mile, undiscounted with no residual value.
Run sensitivities (diesel price, electricity price with and without demand charges, BEV price, kWh/mi, infrastructure cost, incentive on/off) and compute break-evens for the top three drivers.

Test feasibility: 250 mi/day max vs derated real-world range; 500 kWh/day; charge hours at 150 kW (about 3.7 h per truck at 1:1; about 7.4 h per charger at 1:2 in the overnight window); fleet peak MW; utility interconnection lead time for about 1.5 MW against the 30C 30 Jun 2026 in-service date; BEV weight/payload note.
State the plan-level assumptions, risks and go/pilot/wait logic.
Produce an 'Open items for the carrier' list (dwell window, depot return pattern, utility and tariff, tractor spec, depot power and space), each tied to the result it affects.
In a correction round, apply the verifier's corrected inputs, rerun everything and report which numbers changed; always re-emit the full artifact set, even if only passing step 3 through unchanged.

outputs.format: markdown table: cost component | diesel $/truck 7-yr | BEV $/truck 7-yr | difference; plus $/mile row; sensitivity table with break-evens; feasibility list; assumptions list; open-items list (item | result it affects); model script saved to the workspace

success_criteria: Totals reproduce when recomputed independently
Every input traces to the input sheet or register, or is marked as an assumption
Break-even values are stated for the top 3 drivers
Feasibility verdict ties to actual numbers (kWh/day, hours, MW, lead time)
Each open item is tied to the specific result it affects
constraints: Undiscounted, net of incentives, no residual value (per the working interpretation)

created_roles.name: Cost Model Verifier
created_roles.description: Independent reviewer from FP&A or audit who checks that figures match sources, dates are present and arithmetic reproduces. Did not produce any numbers and has no stake in the conclusion.
created_roles.prompt: You are an independent model auditor. You receive the incentive and tax register, the input sheet and the TCO model summary. (1) Re-open the source URLs for the 8 most influential inputs and confirm that value and date match; give the right value where they do not. (2) Re-derive the 7-year totals from the stated inputs with your own arithmetic (calc or a fresh Python snippet written by you, not the modeller's script) and compare. If no code tool is available, use calc step by step and say so. (3) Verify the 45W and 30C determination against the primary source text and confirm the base case counts no uncertain incentive. (4) Check units, the 60,000 x 7 = 420,000 mi basis, charger-ratio math (1:1 and 1:2) and double counting. (5) Confirm every figure has a date. Output: a PASS/FAIL list with evidence per check, then a corrections table (item | found | should be | source | material yes/no). If anything material fails, state which downstream numbers change and give corrected values, and end with 'RERUN REQUIRED'. When called a second time on the modeller's corrected output, recheck only the changed items and the totals and end with 'CLEARED' or the remaining FAILs. If a material FAIL remains after the second rerun, end with 'UNRESOLVED' and list each open item with the best available value, so the memo can label it; do not request a third rerun. Be specific and neutral; do not soften failures.
created_roles.goal: Confirm or correct every number, citation and date in the TCO outputs before the memo is written, including after any correction round.
responsibilities: Spot-check at least the 8 most influential inputs against their source URLs (diesel price, electricity price, both vehicle prices, charger cost, maintenance, 45W status, kWh/mi).
Recompute the TCO totals independently from the stated inputs and compare.
Check that the 45W and 30C conclusions match the primary source and that no incentive is counted that is not claimable.
Check units (cents vs dollars per kWh, per mile vs per year), the 420,000-mile basis, charger-ratio math, and that every figure has a date.
Return a pass/fail list with corrections; classify each FAIL as material (changes a total, the recommendation or an incentive) or minor.

In the re-check round, recompute only the changed totals and confirm the corrected table. After a second round with a material FAIL still open, list the unresolved items for labelling in the memo instead of requesting a third rerun.
inputs: TCO table and model summary (step 3, and step 5 in the re-check round)

outputs.format: list: each check as PASS/FAIL with the evidence, then a table: item | found | should be | source | material? ; then the corrected downstream numbers if anything changed; final status line

success_criteria: Independent recomputation matches totals within rounding, or the discrepancy is explained
Every FAIL has a specific correction
No figure is left without a date and source
Final status is exactly one of CLEARED, RERUN REQUIRED, or UNRESOLVED (with the items listed)
constraints: Must not reuse the modeller's script as the only check; recompute separately

created_roles.name: Memo Editor and Document Assembler
created_roles.description: Executive-communication editor who turns verified analysis into a tight decision memo. Adds no new analysis, only selects, orders and edits. Document building comes through the docx skill, not through analysis tools.
created_roles.prompt: You are the editor who finalises the memo. Use only the upstream artifacts, the cleared model and the verification reports; add no analysis or new numbers. MANDATED LINE (exact string, plain apostrophe in utility's, no backslash): I read "federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026" as Federal 45W commercial clean vehicle credit (up to $40,000 for over 14,000 lb), which may have expired for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025, plus any Indiana state or utility programs; if you meant Grant and rebate programs (EPA Clean Heavy-Duty Vehicles grants, VW settlement funds via IDEM, utility make-ready rebates) or Federal excise tax exemption and other tax treatment such as depreciation, the answer below may not apply. I read "Indiana commercial electricity rate" as EIA average commercial retail price for Indiana in cents/kWh; if you meant A specific utility's commercial or EV tariff (Duke Energy Indiana, AES Indiana, NIPSCO, I&M) including demand charges, the answer below may not apply. I read "7-year total cost of ownership per truck" as Undiscounted sum of purchase, energy, maintenance and infrastructure over 7 years, net of incentives; if you meant Discounted TCO including residual or resale value at year 7, the answer below may not apply.  Steps: (1) Write that string to mandated_line.txt and make it the first paragraph of the document; after building, read the first paragraph back and compare it with the file; stop and fix if they differ. (2) Then: bottom-line recommendation (2-3 sentences: go / pilot / wait, with the reason); TCO table (diesel vs BEV by component, $/truck over 7 yrs and $/mile); feasibility note (250 mi, kWh/day, charging hours, MW, lead time); assumptions (every one, terse) ending with one or two lines of 'Open items for the carrier' (dwell window, depot return pattern, utility and tariff, tractor spec, depot power and space, each with the result it affects); sensitivity/break-even (2-3 lines); one line stating that residual value and discounting could shift the result and that the undiscounted, no-residual definition may favour BEV; numbered sources with publication/as-of dates, cited in-line by number. If the last verification report says UNRESOLVED, label each listed item in the memo as unresolved with its best available value. (3) Build the .docx with the docx skill and its local tools (0.6-0.7 in margins, 9-10 pt); if the skill is unfilled, build with python-docx through whatever local shell is provided; if no document tool exists at all, deliver markdown and state plainly that R11 (the .docx) is unmet. (4) Count pages: convert to PDF with the converter the docx skill provides (for example soffice headless) and count pages; if no converter exists, state that the page count is unverified, give a word and line estimate with a safety margin, and keep the table to 8 rows or fewer. (5) Begin your chat reply with the same mandated line, then name the file.
created_roles.goal: Assemble the final memo (2 pages at most) that opens with the mandated line, shows the verified TCO table, states assumptions, cites every figure with its date and gives the recommendation.
responsibilities: Open with the mandated interpretation line verbatim (stored as a constant in the prompt, written to mandated_line.txt and compared character by character with the first paragraph of the .docx).
Use the final cleared model numbers and apply every correction from the verification report; label any items the verifier left UNRESOLVED.

Fit into 2 pages: recommendation up front, TCO table, short feasibility note, terse assumptions including a one- or two-line 'Open items for the carrier', 2-3 lines of sensitivity/break-even, numbered sources with dates, and a one-line note that residual value and discounting could shift the result and that the undiscounted, no-residual definition may favour BEV.
Build the .docx (0.6-0.7 in margins, 9-10 pt) and verify the page count with the docx skill's local tools.
Begin the chat reply that carries the .docx with the same mandated line.
inputs: TCO table and model summary with open-items list (steps 3 and 5)

outputs.format: memo: Word .docx, at most 2 pages, with sections Recommendation, TCO table, Feasibility, Assumptions (incl. open items), Sensitivity, Sources (with dates)

success_criteria: First paragraph equals the mandated string character for character (programmatic comparison passes)
Table numbers equal the cleared model
Every figure carries an in-line source number and a dated source entry
Residual-value/discounting caveat and open items are present
Page count is 2 or fewer, verified by converter; otherwise labeled 'unverified' with a word/line estimate
constraints: About 1,150 words total including the ~240-word mandated line

## Thought
The question is a 7-year undiscounted TCO comparison, diesel vs battery-electric, for a 20-truck Indiana regional fleet. The answer depends on a handful of figures that must come from dated sources: EIA diesel and Indiana commercial electricity prices, BEV and diesel tractor prices, charger costs, maintenance, and above all the 2026 incentive status. 45W appears to have ended for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025, and 30C for charger property placed in service after 30 Jun 2026. That is a legal and current-events claim to verify, not assume. Operational feasibility (250 mi/day against real BEV range, and overnight charging against the utility's demand charges) can change the recommendation, so it is part of the analysis. The team is two researchers (incentives; costs), a modeller who builds the TCO and sensitivities, an independent verifier, and a summariser for the 2-page docx. The memo must open with the mandated interpretation line and cite every figure with its date.

## Requirements:
R1: Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel vs battery-electric (undiscounted sum of purchase, energy, maintenance and infrastructure, net of incentives).
R2: Establish the purchase price for a diesel Class 8 tractor and a battery-electric Class 8 tractor (dated, sourced).
R3: Determine which federal and Indiana incentives actually apply to a purchase in 2026 (45W status, 30C charger credit, Indiana state, IDEM/VW, EPA grants, utility make-ready programs). State eligibility and the amount applied in the model.
R4: Compute fuel/energy cost per mile: Indiana (or Midwest, if Indiana is unavailable) on-highway diesel price vs Indiana commercial electricity rate, with stated mpg and kWh/mile.
R5: Estimate charging infrastructure cost per truck (about 150 kW DC depot chargers, installation, utility upgrade, shared or 1:1), net of any applicable incentive.
R6: Estimate maintenance cost per mile and over 7 years for both powertrains (dated sources).
R7: Show the TCO table (diesel vs BEV, by cost component, per truck over 7 years, plus per mile).
R8: State every assumption.
R9: Cite every figure with its source and date.
R10: Give a recommendation, including operational feasibility of 250 mi/day and a short sensitivity or break-even on the drivers that could flip it.
R11: Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.
R12: Open the final answer with the mandated interpretation line, verbatim.

## Givens and Assumptions:
- given: 20 Class 8 tractors; regional routes under 250 mi/day; about 60,000 mi/truck/yr; Indiana; 7-year horizon; purchase in 2026.
- derived: 7-yr miles per truck = 60,000 × 7 = 420,000; fleet miles/yr = 60,000 × 20 = 1,200,000.
- derived: operating days ≈ 60,000 / 250 = 240 days/yr (so 250 mi is the upper bound on a day; the average may be lower).
- derived: BEV energy at 2.0 kWh/mi (assumption, to be replaced by a sourced range of about 1.6–2.3) = 120,000 kWh/yr at the vehicle, 840,000 kWh over 7 yrs. Grid kWh is higher by charger losses (assume about 90% efficiency → ÷0.9).
- derived: daily need at the max route = 250 × 2.0 = 500 kWh; at 150 kW that is about 3.3 h of charging (about 3.7 h with losses), so overnight charging is feasible. One 150 kW charger can serve 2 trucks with dual ports and load management, so 10 chargers for 20 trucks (1.5 MW) vs 20 chargers (3 MW).
- derived: diesel use at 6.5 mpg (assumption, sourced range of about 6–7.5) = 60,000 / 6.5 ≈ 9,231 gal/yr and 420,000 / 6.5 ≈ 64,615 gal over 7 yrs.
- derived: cost per mile = diesel $/gal ÷ mpg; electricity $/kWh × kWh/mi ÷ 0.9 (plus a demand-charge adder per mile = monthly demand $ ÷ miles).
- derived: per-truck infrastructure = (chargers × installed cost + utility upgrade − incentives) ÷ 20.
- assumption: BEV range under real-world load, weather and aging (the 250 mi/day maximum vs a rated 230–500 mi depending on model) is adequate for a sourced model, or else the recommendation is flagged as route-dependent.
- assumption: prices are in nominal 2026 dollars held flat for the base case; the model also runs escalators (diesel and electricity ±) as sensitivity. Undiscounted, no residual value, no financing, no tax depreciation (as the working interpretation states).
- assumption: federal excise tax (12% on new heavy trucks) applies to both and is included in the purchase price or noted as equal. Indiana registration/EV fee differences are included only if a source shows a material amount.
- assumption: no battery replacement within 7 yrs / 420,000 mi unless the warranty source says otherwise. Check warranty terms (typical 8 yr / 500,000 mi).
- assumption: day cab/sleeper unspecified, so use a representative day-cab or regional-haul tractor for each powertrain and state the model names.
- assumption: base case uses the Indiana commercial average rate from EIA plus a separate stated demand-charge sensitivity, because the working interpretation uses the EIA average and not a specific tariff.

## Risks and Decisions:
- 45W/30C status is the biggest legal uncertainty. If a primary source contradicts the expected cutoff (45W: acquired after 30 Sep 2025; 30C: placed in service after 30 Jun 2026), the verifier flags it and step 3 reruns with the corrected incentive. The base case counts $0 for any incentive that is not near-certain.
- Demand charges could erase the BEV energy advantage and the EIA average hides them. Decision at step 3: if the demand-charge sensitivity flips the result, the recommendation is "pilot" and the memo says a tariff-specific quote is needed.
- Range and payload: if the derated real-world range of the chosen BEV is under 250 mi, the recommendation is limited to the routes that fit or to a higher-range model (e.g. Tesla Semi), and the model reruns with that price.
- BEV tractor prices vary a lot and are often quote-only. Use ranges, label the type (list, quote, study), and show the break-even price.
- Indiana-specific diesel price may not be published weekly. Use the EIA Midwest figure and say so. If the live fetch fails, use the latest cached EIA value with its date.
- The docx skill or page counter may stay unfilled. Fallback: the summariser delivers markdown within the length budget, and the TCO Modeller can render it with python-docx via Bash if a follow-up pass is allowed. Length is controlled by a word budget of about 900 words.
- Scope: the undiscounted, no-residual-value definition favours BEV, because battery residual is ignored and cheaper energy accumulates. The memo notes in one line that residual value and discounting could shift the result, as the mandated opening line already signals.

- 60,000 / 250 = 240 operating days.
- 2.0 kWh/mi gives 120,000 kWh per year and 840,000 kWh over 7 years.

- 6.5 mpg gives 9,231 gal per year and 64,615 gal over 7 years.

- The Risks section says that if 45W or 30C differs from expectation, "the verifier flags it and step 3 reruns". No such rerun step or loop exists in the plan.
- Step 4 supplies "corrected downstream numbers" and step 5 applies them. Step 5, however, is forbidden from doing new analysis. A changed incentive or input would need a full model rerun, and nobody re-verifies it.

## Thought
The task is a 7-year undiscounted TCO comparison, diesel vs battery-electric, for 20 Indiana regional tractors. It turns on a few dated inputs: EIA diesel and Indiana commercial electricity prices, tractor prices, charger costs and maintenance. The 2026 incentive status is also a legal question to verify, not assume; 45W may have ended for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025. Operational feasibility (250 mi/day against derated range, charging windows, utility capacity and lead time) can change the answer, so the modeller tests it. This revision adds a correction loop (rerun and re-verify when the verifier finds a material FAIL). The editor can now build the .docx through python-docx even if the docx skill is unfilled. The mandated line is held as an exact string and compared character by character. Powertrain-specific taxes and fees sit in one step. The quality-gate numbers and phrases are now carried by requirements and givens.

## Requirements:
R1: Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel vs battery-electric (undiscounted sum of purchase, energy, maintenance and infrastructure, net of incentives).
R2: Establish the purchase price of a new diesel Class 8 tractor and of a battery-electric Class 8 tractor (dated, sourced, with the type of price labeled).
R3: Determine which federal and Indiana incentives actually apply to a purchase in 2026 (45W, 30C, Indiana state, IDEM/VW, EPA grants, utility make-ready). State eligibility and the amount used in the model.
R4: Compute fuel/energy cost per mile: Indiana (or Midwest) on-highway diesel price vs the EIA Indiana commercial electricity rate, with stated mpg and kWh/mile.
R5: Estimate charging infrastructure cost per truck (about 150 kW DC depot chargers, installation, utility upgrade, 1:1 and shared 1:2), net of any applicable incentive.
R6: Estimate maintenance cost per mile and over 7 years for both powertrains (dated sources) and carry it in the model.
R7: Show the TCO table (diesel vs BEV by component, per truck over 7 years, plus $/mile).
R8: State every assumption.
R9: Cite every figure with its source and date.
R10: Give a recommendation, including feasibility of 250 mi/day and a short sensitivity or break-even on the drivers that could flip it.
R11: Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.
R12: Open the final answer (the memo and the chat reply carrying it) with the mandated interpretation line, verbatim.
R13: Model the carrier's operation as stated: a fleet that runs 20 Class 8 tractors on regional routes under 250 miles a day, about 60,000 miles per truck per year, in Indiana.
R14: Plan the work as a lead would before staffing it: pin down the objective and deliverables, work out the numbers, surface assumptions and risks, and build in checks (shown by the assumptions list, the risk decisions and the verification report).
R15: Read "federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026" as Federal 45W (up to $40,000 for over 14,000 lb, possibly expired for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025) plus any Indiana state or utility programs.
R16: Read "Indiana commercial electricity rate" as the EIA average commercial retail price for Indiana in cents/kWh.
R17: Read "7-year total cost of ownership per truck" as the undiscounted sum of purchase, energy, maintenance and infrastructure over 7 years, net of incentives.

## Givens and Assumptions:
- given: 20 Class 8 tractors; regional routes under 250 mi/day; about 60,000 mi/truck/yr; Indiana; 7-year horizon; purchase in 2026.
- given: Class 8 means over 33,000 lb GVWR, sleeper or day cab unspecified.
- given: 45W commercial clean vehicle credit is up to $40,000 for vehicles over 14,000 lb, and may have expired for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025 (to be verified against primary text). The 2025 date comes from the post-reconciliation-act 45W termination.
- derived: 7-yr miles per truck = 60,000 × 7 = 420,000; fleet miles/yr = 60,000 × 20 = 1,200,000.
- derived: operating days ≈ 60,000 / 250 = 240 days/yr, so 250 mi is an upper bound on a day.
- derived: BEV energy at 2.0 kWh/mi (assumption, to be replaced by a sourced range of about 1.6–2.3) = 120,000 kWh/yr at the vehicle and 840,000 kWh over 7 yrs. Grid kWh = vehicle kWh ÷ 0.9.
- derived: max-route daily need = 250 × 2.0 = 500 kWh. At 150 kW that is 500 / 150 ≈ 3.3 h, or 3.7 h with losses (÷0.9).
- derived: at 1:2 sharing, one charger serves 2 trucks = 1,000 kWh / 150 kW ≈ 6.7 h, or 7.4 h with losses. That fits a roughly 10 h overnight window only with load management. Fleet peak = 10 chargers × 150 kW = 1.5 MW at 1:2, or 20 × 150 kW = 3.0 MW at 1:1.
- derived: diesel at 6.5 mpg (assumption, sourced range of about 6–7.5) = 60,000 / 6.5 ≈ 9,231 gal/yr and 420,000 / 6.5 ≈ 64,615 gal over 7 yrs.
- derived: cost per mile: diesel $/gal ÷ mpg; BEV $/kWh × kWh/mi ÷ 0.9, plus a demand-charge adder (monthly demand $ × 12 ÷ 60,000 mi per truck).
- derived: infrastructure per truck = (chargers × installed cost + utility upgrade − incentives) ÷ 20.
- assumption: prices are in nominal 2026 dollars held flat in the base case, with escalators as sensitivities. Undiscounted, no residual value, no financing, no depreciation (per the working interpretation).
- assumption: the 12% federal excise tax on new heavy trucks is checked by the incentives/taxes researcher. It is included in both prices or noted as equal, and Indiana fees are included only if a source shows a material powertrain difference.
- assumption: no battery replacement within 7 yrs / 420,000 mi unless the warranty source says otherwise (typical 8 yr / 500,000 mi, to be checked).
- assumption: a representative regional-haul tractor is used for each powertrain, with model names stated.
- assumption: the base case uses the EIA Indiana commercial average rate. A demand-charge adder is shown as a separate sensitivity.
- assumption: BEV tractor weight/payload penalty is noted qualitatively, not monetized, unless a source gives a figure.
- assumption: the memo budget is about 1,150 words in total, including the roughly 240-word mandated opening line (so about 900 words of body and table), at 9–10 pt with 0.6–0.7 in margins.

## Risks and Decisions:
- 45W/30C status is the biggest legal uncertainty. If a primary source contradicts the expected cutoffs (45W: acquired after 30 Sep 2025; 30C: in service after 30 Jun 2026), the verifier flags a material FAIL, step 5 reruns with the corrected incentive and step 6 re-checks before the memo is written. The base case counts $0 for anything not near-certain.
- Demand charges can erase the BEV energy advantage and the EIA average hides them. Decision at step 3/5: if the demand-charge sensitivity flips the result, the recommendation is "pilot" and the memo says a tariff-specific quote is needed.
- Range, payload and charging window: if the derated BEV range is under 250 mi, limit the recommendation to routes that fit or to a higher-range model and rerun with that price. If 1:2 sharing (about 7.4 h per charger) does not fit the overnight dwell, use 1:1 and its higher infrastructure cost.
- Utility interconnection lead time for about 1.5–3 MW may exceed the 30C in-service cutoff. Treat 30C as upside only, and flag the lead time as a schedule risk.
- BEV tractor prices vary widely and are often quote-only. Use ranges, label the type and show the break-even price.
- Indiana-only diesel may not be published weekly: use EIA Midwest and say so. If a live fetch fails, use the latest cached EIA value with its date.
- If a tool is unfilled: the modeller falls back to calc ("calc-only, no script saved"). The verifier uses calc step by step. The editor builds with python-docx via Bash. Markdown is the last resort, with R11 explicitly flagged as unmet.
- Scope bias: the undiscounted, no-residual definition may favour BEV (cheaper energy accumulates, battery residual is ignored). The memo carries a one-line note on this.

rounds.planner_raw:
## Thought
The task is a 7-year undiscounted TCO comparison of diesel and battery-electric tractors for 20 Indiana regional trucks. It depends on a few dated inputs: EIA diesel and Indiana commercial electricity prices, tractor prices, charger costs and maintenance. The 2026 incentive status (45W, 30C) is a legal question to verify against primary sources, not assume. Feasibility (250 mi/day against derated range, charging window, 1.5–3 MW utility capacity and lead time) can change the answer, so the modeller tests it. This revision applies the reviewer's plan suggestions:
- Step 5 now always outputs the full artifact set.
- Step 6 depends on steps 1, 2, 4 and 5, with a bounded exit after two rerun rounds.
- Step 7 carries the residual-value and discounting caveat and an "Open items for the carrier" list.

It also fixes the quality-gate problem: the summariser now has an empty tools list and owns only step 7. Document building comes through the docx skill, which brings its own local tools.

## Requirements:
R1: Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel vs battery-electric (undiscounted sum of purchase, energy, maintenance and infrastructure, net of incentives).
R2: Establish the purchase price of a new diesel Class 8 tractor and of a battery-electric Class 8 tractor (dated, sourced, with the price type labeled).
R3: Determine which federal and Indiana incentives actually apply to a purchase in 2026 (45W, 30C, Indiana state, IDEM/VW, EPA grants, utility make-ready). State eligibility and the amount used in the model.
R4: Compute fuel/energy cost per mile: Indiana (or Midwest) on-highway diesel price vs the EIA Indiana commercial electricity rate, with stated mpg and kWh/mile.
R5: Estimate charging infrastructure cost per truck (about 150 kW DC depot chargers, installation, utility upgrade, 1:1 and shared 1:2), net of any applicable incentive.
R6: Estimate maintenance cost per mile and over 7 years for both powertrains (dated sources) and carry it in the model.
R7: Show the TCO table (diesel vs BEV by component, per truck over 7 years, plus $/mile).
R8: State every assumption.
R9: Cite every figure with its source and date.
R10: Give a recommendation, including feasibility of 250 mi/day, a short sensitivity or break-even on the drivers that could flip it, and a one-line note that residual value and discounting could shift the result (the undiscounted, no-residual definition may favour BEV).
R11: Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.
R12: Open the final answer (the memo and the chat reply carrying it) with the mandated interpretation line, verbatim.
R13: Model the carrier's operation as stated: a fleet that runs 20 Class 8 tractors on regional routes under 250 miles a day, about 60,000 miles per truck per year, in Indiana.
R14: Plan the work as a lead would before staffing it: pin down the objective and deliverables, work out the numbers, surface assumptions and risks, and build in checks (shown by the assumptions list, the risk decisions and the verification report).
R15: Read "federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026" as Federal 45W (up to $40,000 for over 14,000 lb, possibly expired for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025) plus any Indiana state or utility programs.
R16: Read "Indiana commercial electricity rate" as the EIA average commercial retail price for Indiana in cents/kWh.
R17: Read "7-year total cost of ownership per truck" as the undiscounted sum of purchase, energy, maintenance and infrastructure over 7 years, net of incentives.
R18: Provide an "Open items for the carrier" list (dwell window, depot return pattern, utility and tariff, tractor spec, depot power and space), each tied to the result it affects, and carry it into the memo's Assumptions section in one or two lines.

## Givens and Assumptions:
- given: 20 Class 8 tractors; regional routes under 250 mi/day; about 60,000 mi/truck/yr; Indiana; 7-year horizon; purchase in 2026.
- given: Class 8 means over 33,000 lb GVWR, sleeper or day cab unspecified.
- given: the 45W commercial clean vehicle credit is up to $40,000 for vehicles over 14,000 lb, and may have expired for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025 (to be verified against primary text). The 2025 date comes from the post-reconciliation-act 45W termination.
- derived: 7-yr miles per truck = 60,000 × 7 = 420,000; fleet miles/yr = 60,000 × 20 = 1,200,000.
- derived: operating days ≈ 60,000 / 250 = 240 days/yr, so 250 mi is an upper bound on a day.
- derived: BEV energy at 2.0 kWh/mi (assumption, to be replaced by a sourced range of about 1.6–2.3) = 120,000 kWh/yr at the vehicle and 840,000 kWh over 7 yrs. Grid kWh = vehicle kWh ÷ 0.9.
- derived: max-route daily need = 250 × 2.0 = 500 kWh. At 150 kW that is 500 / 150 ≈ 3.3 h, or 3.7 h with losses (÷0.9).
- derived: at 1:2 sharing, one charger serves 2 trucks = 1,000 kWh / 150 kW ≈ 6.7 h, or 7.4 h with losses. That fits a roughly 10 h overnight window only with load management. Fleet peak = 10 × 150 kW = 1.5 MW at 1:2, or 20 × 150 kW = 3.0 MW at 1:1.
- derived: diesel at 6.5 mpg (assumption, sourced range of about 6–7.5) = 60,000 / 6.5 ≈ 9,231 gal/yr and 420,000 / 6.5 ≈ 64,615 gal over 7 yrs.
- derived: cost per mile: diesel $/gal ÷ mpg; BEV $/kWh × kWh/mi ÷ 0.9, plus a demand-charge adder (monthly demand $ × 12 ÷ 60,000 mi per truck).
- derived: infrastructure per truck = (chargers × installed cost + utility upgrade − incentives) ÷ 20.
- assumption: prices are in nominal 2026 dollars held flat in the base case, with escalators as sensitivities. Undiscounted, no residual value, no financing, no depreciation (per the working interpretation).
- assumption: the 12% federal excise tax on new heavy trucks is checked by the incentives/taxes researcher. It is included in both prices or noted as equal, and Indiana fees are included only if a source shows a material powertrain difference.
- assumption: no battery replacement within 7 yrs / 420,000 mi unless the warranty source says otherwise (typical 8 yr / 500,000 mi, to be checked).
- assumption: a representative regional-haul tractor is used for each powertrain, with model names stated.
- assumption: the base case uses the EIA Indiana commercial average rate. A demand-charge adder is shown as a separate sensitivity.
- assumption: BEV tractor weight/payload penalty is noted qualitatively, not monetized, unless a source gives a figure.
- assumption: the memo budget is about 1,150 words in total, including the roughly 240-word mandated opening line (so about 900 words of body and table), at 9–10 pt with 0.6–0.7 in margins.
- assumption: the correction loop is bounded. Steps 5 and 6 run at most twice. If a material FAIL remains after the second round, the memo proceeds with the unresolved items labelled as such.

## Open Questions:
- question: Which utility serves the depot (Duke Energy Indiana, AES Indiana, NIPSCO, I&M) and what is its demand-charge tariff? | assumption: use the EIA Indiana commercial average as the base, with a demand-charge sensitivity; flagged as the main uncertainty (a tariff-specific quote is needed).
- question: Does the fleet already have 1.5–3 MW of service capacity and a depot site with space for chargers? | assumption: include a sourced utility-upgrade allowance range and flag it.
- question: Day cab or sleeper, and which tractor spec? | assumption: not specified; model a representative regional-haul tractor and say so.
- question: What is the overnight dwell window, and do all trucks return to the depot each night? | assumption: about 10 h overnight at the depot, all trucks returning daily; flagged as an open item for the carrier.
- question: Is an Indiana-only weekly diesel price published? | assumption: if not, use the EIA Midwest (PADD 2) weekly on-highway price and state it.

## Risks and Decisions:
- 45W/30C status is the biggest legal uncertainty. If a primary source contradicts the expected cutoffs (45W: acquired after 30 Sep 2025; 30C: in service after 30 Jun 2026), the verifier flags a material FAIL, step 5 reruns with the corrected incentive and step 6 re-checks before the memo is written. The base case counts $0 for anything not near-certain.
- The correction loop is bounded. After the second RERUN REQUIRED (steps 5 and 6 run twice at most), the work proceeds to step 7 with the unresolved items labelled in the memo, so the loop cannot stall delivery.
- Demand charges can erase the BEV energy advantage and the EIA average hides them. Decision at steps 3 and 5: if the demand-charge sensitivity flips the result, the recommendation is "pilot" and the memo says a tariff-specific quote is needed.
- Range, payload and charging window: if the derated BEV range is under 250 mi, limit the recommendation to routes that fit or to a higher-range model and rerun with that price. If 1:2 sharing (about 7.4 h per charger) does not fit the overnight dwell, use 1:1 and its higher infrastructure cost.
- Utility interconnection lead time for about 1.5–3 MW may exceed the 30C in-service cutoff. Treat 30C as upside only, and flag the lead time as a schedule risk.
- BEV tractor prices vary widely and are often quote-only. Use ranges, label the price type and show the break-even price.
- Indiana-only diesel may not be published weekly: use EIA Midwest and say so. If a live fetch fails, use the latest cached EIA value with its date.
- Open items that only the carrier can supply (dwell window, depot return pattern, utility and tariff, tractor spec, depot power and space) are not guessed. They are listed in the memo with the result each one affects.
- If a tool is unfilled: the modeller falls back to calc ("calc-only, no script saved"). The verifier uses calc step by step. The editor builds with python-docx through the docx skill's local shell. Markdown is the last resort, with R11 explicitly flagged as unmet.
- Scope bias: the undiscounted, no-residual definition may favour BEV, because cheaper energy accumulates and battery residual is ignored. The memo carries a one-line note on this.

givens: given: 20 Class 8 tractors; regional routes under 250 mi/day; about 60,000 mi/truck/yr; Indiana; 7-year horizon; purchase in 2026.
given: Class 8 means over 33,000 lb GVWR, sleeper or day cab unspecified.

given: the 45W commercial clean vehicle credit is up to $40,000 for vehicles over 14,000 lb, and may have expired for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025 (to be verified against primary text). The 2025 date comes from the post-reconciliation-act 45W termination.
derived: 7-yr miles per truck = 60,000 × 7 = 420,000; fleet miles/yr = 60,000 × 20 = 1,200,000.
derived: operating days ≈ 60,000 / 250 = 240 days/yr, so 250 mi is an upper bound on a day.
derived: BEV energy at 2.0 kWh/mi (assumption, to be replaced by a sourced range of about 1.6–2.3) = 120,000 kWh/yr at the vehicle and 840,000 kWh over 7 yrs. Grid kWh = vehicle kWh ÷ 0.9.
derived: max-route daily need = 250 × 2.0 = 500 kWh. At 150 kW that is 500 / 150 ≈ 3.3 h, or 3.7 h with losses (÷0.9).

derived: at 1:2 sharing, one charger serves 2 trucks = 1,000 kWh / 150 kW ≈ 6.7 h, or 7.4 h with losses. That fits a roughly 10 h overnight window only with load management. Fleet peak = 10 × 150 kW = 1.5 MW at 1:2, or 20 × 150 kW = 3.0 MW at 1:1.
derived: diesel at 6.5 mpg (assumption, sourced range of about 6–7.5) = 60,000 / 6.5 ≈ 9,231 gal/yr and 420,000 / 6.5 ≈ 64,615 gal over 7 yrs.
derived: cost per mile: diesel $/gal ÷ mpg; BEV $/kWh × kWh/mi ÷ 0.9, plus a demand-charge adder (monthly demand $ × 12 ÷ 60,000 mi per truck).
derived: infrastructure per truck = (chargers × installed cost + utility upgrade − incentives) ÷ 20.

assumption: prices are in nominal 2026 dollars held flat in the base case, with escalators as sensitivities. Undiscounted, no residual value, no financing, no depreciation (per the working interpretation).

assumption: the 12% federal excise tax on new heavy trucks is checked by the incentives/taxes researcher. It is included in both prices or noted as equal, and Indiana fees are included only if a source shows a material powertrain difference.
assumption: no battery replacement within 7 yrs / 420,000 mi unless the warranty source says otherwise (typical 8 yr / 500,000 mi, to be checked).
assumption: a representative regional-haul tractor is used for each powertrain, with model names stated.
assumption: the base case uses the EIA Indiana commercial average rate. A demand-charge adder is shown as a separate sensitivity.
assumption: BEV tractor weight/payload penalty is noted qualitatively, not monetized, unless a source gives a figure.
assumption: the memo budget is about 1,150 words in total, including the roughly 240-word mandated opening line (so about 900 words of body and table), at 9–10 pt with 0.6–0.7 in margins.
assumption: the correction loop is bounded. Steps 5 and 6 run at most twice. If a material FAIL remains after the second round, the memo proceeds with the unresolved items labelled as such.
risks: 45W/30C status is the biggest legal uncertainty. If a primary source contradicts the expected cutoffs (45W: acquired after 30 Sep 2025; 30C: in service after 30 Jun 2026), the verifier flags a material FAIL, step 5 reruns with the corrected incentive and step 6 re-checks before the memo is written. The base case counts $0 for anything not near-certain.

The correction loop is bounded. After the second RERUN REQUIRED (steps 5 and 6 run twice at most), the work proceeds to step 7 with the unresolved items labelled in the memo, so the loop cannot stall delivery.

Demand charges can erase the BEV energy advantage and the EIA average hides them. Decision at steps 3 and 5: if the demand-charge sensitivity flips the result, the recommendation is "pilot" and the memo says a tariff-specific quote is needed.

Range, payload and charging window: if the derated BEV range is under 250 mi, limit the recommendation to routes that fit or to a higher-range model and rerun with that price. If 1:2 sharing (about 7.4 h per charger) does not fit the overnight dwell, use 1:1 and its higher infrastructure cost.
Utility interconnection lead time for about 1.5–3 MW may exceed the 30C in-service cutoff. Treat 30C as upside only, and flag the lead time as a schedule risk.
BEV tractor prices vary widely and are often quote-only. Use ranges, label the price type and show the break-even price.
Indiana-only diesel may not be published weekly: use EIA Midwest and say so. If a live fetch fails, use the latest cached EIA value with its date.

Open items that only the carrier can supply (dwell window, depot return pattern, utility and tariff, tractor spec, depot power and space) are not guessed. They are listed in the memo with the result each one affects.

If a tool is unfilled: the modeller falls back to calc ("calc-only, no script saved"). The verifier uses calc step by step. The editor builds with python-docx through the docx skill's local shell. Markdown is the last resort, with R11 explicitly flagged as unmet.
Scope bias: the undiscounted, no-residual definition may favour BEV, because cheaper energy accumulates and battery residual is ignored. The memo carries a one-line note on this.
